Crucially, this upward pressure on real rates is independent of how the CapEx is financed — debt, retained earnings or equity all consume the same real resources. The financing channel matters for asset prices and risk allocation but not for the macroeconomic arithmetic linking saving, investment and equilibrium real rates.

headline: The 52-week high is an irrational anchor: professional investors buy what retail investors sell near that level

The rational alternative is to anchor on intrinsic value or a relevant valuation ratio such as P/E, not the nominal price paid.

He contrasts this favourably with gold, credit and unlisted assets, which lack liquidity and convexity in a crisis.

Secondly and importantly, you actually know your downside risk with an option, which is just simply the price of putting it on. Thirdly, put options are highly liquid in a sell-off. And that's important because the protection you've enjoyed can be monetized quickly when volatility or equities really are oversold. And with options you can hold more equities over the cycle for the same level of portfolio risk. So you put all that together, it's good for returns.

reasoning: Net issuance for long-maturity bonds from non-AI corporates contracted materially in 2025 and year-to-date, which could initially appear to be crowding out. However, corporate borrowers are not passive takers of the maturity structure; they actively time issuance, favouring shorter maturities when long-dated yields are elevated. The academic literature supports this: companies adjust the duration of supply in response to government changes in duration pricing. The contraction in long-end issuance therefore reflects rational corporate finance decisions under a high long-yield environment, not hyperscaler-specific displacement.

For them, this maturity choice is a real corporate finance decision shaped by the trade-off between locking and funding and preserving flexibility. The academic literature also shows that, at the aggregate level, corporate borrowers have tended to adjust the amount of duration they supply when the government changes the amount or price of duration in the market. Simply put, companies manage duration actively, so a decline in long-end issuance does not automatically mean they have been crowded out, especially in the current environment where long-dated yields have risen materially.

He questions the RBA's self-assessment that it is 'well placed' to deal with current challenges, suggesting the board would be better positioned if inflation were already closer to target. He believes the RBA needs to recommit to prioritising inflation control.
quote: I think the key thing that the RBA keeps repeating is that the the board is well placed to deal with the challenges we face at the moment. And I guess the question I have is, are you really that well placed? Would it not be the case that you'd be better placed if inflation was already closer to target? And and so should it now not be the case that actually we're really convinced that you need to focus mostly on keeping inflation, inflation as close to target as often as possible rather than, you know, focusing on the full employment mandate more heavily, which is what I think they've been doing over the last few years.
episode_title: Why Paul thinks the RBA needs to hone in on inflation first and foremost

headline: Government fuel excise cuts act as fiscal stimulus by offsetting higher fuel prices, preventing the price mechanism from naturally slowing inflation
reasoning: Bloxham explains that higher fuel prices would ordinarily reduce consumer spending elsewhere, putting downward pressure on broader inflation. When the government reduces fuel excise to offset high prices, it provides households with more income to spend, which is effectively fiscal stimulus that works against the inflation-dampening mechanism. This means government intervention can inadvertently sustain inflationary pressures.
quote: One of the things we noted, you know, when the government was sort of reducing excise, was that actually that is a form of fiscal stimulus. Like if you have fewer, higher fuel prices, but the government offsets it, they're giving you more income to spend. So in principle, actually you're not letting the mechanism actually work to lower inflation.
episode_title: Why Paul thinks the RBA needs to hone in on inflation first and foremost

headline: Australia's productivity growth has been dismal and is the real constraint on the economy's speed limit, not just fiscal policy; lifting productivity is key to sustainably higher living standards
reasoning: Bloxham argues that while public spending does contribute to demand and inflation, the more fundamental issue is that Australia's economy has a much lower speed limit than in the past due to very weak productivity growth — essentially flat or slightly negative on labour productivity over the past year. He says that if productivity improved, the economy could grow faster without generating as much inflation. He frames this as where policy focus really needs to be, rather than solely blaming fiscal spending, and ties it directly to the RBA being left to do the heavy lifting by pushing the economy into a bigger downturn.
quote: I think I tend to focus and say, well, that's part of it. But the other part of it is actually the economy has a much, much lower speed limit right now than it's had in the past. Productivity growth has been dismal. It's been very, very weak, basically flat a little bit, you know, down a little bit on labor productivity over the past year. So that is where we really need the focus to be. That's how we lift living standards. That's how we're able to grow the economy faster. That would mean that actually inflation wouldn't be as high for the sort of low growth rates we're already seeing in the economy.
episode_title: Why Paul thinks the RBA needs to hone in on inflation first and foremost

headline: Expects RBA to hike in September and again in November, taking cash rate to 4.85%, citing inflation too high and growth too strong relative to Australia's low speed limit
reasoning: Paul Bloxham argues that the RBA has little choice but to raise rates, as inflation remains well above target and economic growth is too strong for an economy with a low productivity-constrained speed limit. He expects the Q3 trimmed mean CPI print to surprise the RBA to the upside, making a November follow-up hike very likely. He also notes that global inflation risks are skewed to the upside, partly due to Middle East conflict. He acknowledges two more hikes will weaken the economy but sees that as the necessary mechanism to bring inflation back to the 2.5% target. He is less convinced than some (e.g. Warren Hogan) that more than two additional hikes will be needed, though he sees risks in both directions.
quote: Well that's our view. I mean we had that we had that view for a while now that we were going to get a rate hike in September, which is today. And we think that they're going to follow up with another hike in November. I guess we get there because inflation is too high, growth is too strong for an economy that's got a very low speed limit at the moment. And so I don't think the RBA has a lot of choices to be able to, to deal with this bike lift, but lifting rates, the global environment has higher interest rates as well. And the global inflation story is looking like it's got more upside risks than downside risks, particularly given what's going on in the Middle East conflict at the moment.
episode_title: Why Paul thinks the RBA needs to hone in on inflation first and foremost

headline: Q3 trimmed mean CPI likely to surprise RBA to the upside, making a November hike very hard to avoid

headline: Division 296 now law: additional 15% tax on super earnings above $3M and 10% above $10M, effective from 30 June 2027 measurement date
reasoning: The Division 296 legislation was passed through Parliament in March 2026 after two years of debate. It imposes an additional 15% tax on the proportion of earnings attributable to superannuation balances exceeding $3 million, and a further 10% on balances exceeding $10 million, bringing effective tax rates to 30% and 40% respectively on those proportions. The thresholds will be CPI-indexed at certain increments. The first measurement year is transitional, with balances assessed at 30 June 2027; from 1 July 2027 onwards, the higher of the opening or closing balance for the financial year determines whether a member is subject to the tax. The tax is levied on the individual rather than the fund, so members can elect to pay it personally or have their super fund pay it, providing cash flow flexibility.
quote: Division 296 will apply to individuals that have total superannuation balances at the start of the financial year or at the end of the financial year that exceeds $3 million. However, there is good news, the 2026-2027 financial year is a transitional year for division 296 purposes. What that means is in the first year, the total super balance will be in reference to the members closing balance as at 30 June 2027. So, if at 30 June 2027, a member across all the superannuation interest has a balance less than $3 million, they won't be subject to the division 296 tax.

headline: Government spending, not corporate greed, is the real driver of inflation — public-sector buyers are price-insensitive, pushing costs economy-wide
reasoning: The speaker argues that claims of 'greedflation' — businesses inflating profits causing inflation — are misplaced. Companies can only charge what consumers are willing to pay, so rising profits reflect consumer willingness to pay higher prices. The root cause is government spending: when government acts as both buyer and seller of services and hands grants to private enterprises, those recipients are not price-sensitive and simply pay whatever is asked, injecting non-market-priced dollars into the economy and driving inflation.
quote: One of the things, you know, that's probably come out recently is this idea that the inflation was caused by businesses making more profit. And there's nonsense around that. What what the idea is that companies are charging more, therefore they're collecting all the cash, therefore that's the driver of inflation. Companies can only charge what consumers are willing to pay. If consumers are willing to pay higher prices, then they'll achieve higher profits. But, ultimately, it starts and finishes with the demand out of the buy side, not the sell side, when it comes to companies. So, then you go, 'Well, why are all these companies making excess profits?' And again, it comes back to government spending, because if a government has a blank checkbook, and it sets the price as both the seller of the service and the buyer of the service.

headline: Sydney and Melbourne price weakness is a valuation story not a credit story: no forced selling, and stress concentrated in high-value top-quartile properties largely absent from RMBS pools
reasoning: The composition of the decline matters more than its size. There are no material forced sales — transaction volumes have fallen because buyers are pausing and sellers are refusing lower prices, meaning losses (which require distressed sales) are not being crystallised. Additionally, the price falls are concentrated in the top quartile of high-value properties, whereas the average mortgage in held deals is $750,000 with concentration limits capping exposure above $2.5 million, so the most stressed segment is largely absent from the pools.
quote: Our view is that the composition of this decline matters much more than its size, and two features make it a valuation story rather than a credit story. First, nobody's being forced to sell. Transaction volumes have fallen because buyers are pausing expecting lower prices, while sellers are refusing to accept lower prices. We're not seeing any material full increase in forced sales. That's important because losses in a mortgage pool come from distressed sales, where a lender has to realize the property at a discount. They don't come from valuations drifting lower while the owner keeps paying. Second, the weakness largely sits outside the pools. The falls in Sydney and Melbourne are concentrated in high-value property, the top quartile. The average mortgage in the deals we hold is $750,000, and concentration limits cap exposure loans above 2 and 1/2 million.

reasoning: Australian RMBS carries a spread of roughly 3.5% versus the broader market (per S&P spin data). The realised loss rate on Australian-rated RMBS — both prime and non-conforming — is zero across all historical episodes including the GFC. The instruments are floating-rate notes whose coupons reset to bank bill swap rate, meaning there is no interest rate duration risk; only credit spread can move the price. In the March Iran-conflict risk-off event, when the S&P/ASX 200 fell nearly 8% and the S&P 500 fell ~5%, the fund's RMBS holdings moved less than 0.5% in capital price and delivered a positive total return, as spread widening was partly offset by higher BBSW and coupon income.
quote: These are floating-rate notes because the coupons reset the bank bill swap rate. No There's no interest rate duration or reprice. The only thing that can move the price is credit spread. And in a period like March, any spread widening is partly offset by higher BBSW or bank bill swap rate and the ongoing coupon income. It's also worth remembering that these figures are price movements only. And as we saw in the earlier slide, in the month after the May budget, those same holdings recovered and moved higher despite the new structural risk to housing.

headline: Selective RMBS investing with rigorous deal-by-deal stress testing; rejecting roughly 40% of deals keeps portfolio arrears at 2.59% versus 3.5% for the broader market
reasoning: The investment process involves a three-step loan-level analysis: forecasting arrears and foreclosure rates on every individual mortgage, running foreclosures through each deal's cash flow structure to ensure full repayment of every tranche, and applying a binary approval gate where any forecast of capital loss prohibits investment. Approximately one-third of deals reviewed are rejected, with four in ten failing due to forecast cash flow losses. This disciplined selection has produced portfolio arrears of 2.59% versus 3.5% for the broader RMBS market and zero losses across historical stress episodes. The speaker presents this as a reflection of process quality rather than a shortage of supply, as rejected deals remain available for purchase.
quote: Every deal is stress tested before you can buy it. It's a three-step process. First, we analyze the pool loan by loan, forecasting arrears and foreclosure rates on every individual mortgage. Second, we run those foreclosures through the deal's cash flow structure to test that every layer of the capital stack is repaid in full over the life of the deal. And third, it's a binary decision. If the model forecasts a capital loss, the deal isn't approved, and portfolio managers are prohibited from investing in that particular deal... We only approve about 2/3 of what we look at. So, four in 10 deals fail because of the forecast on cash flow loss. Those rejected deals are available to buy. This is a reflection process, not a shortage of supply. We just don't invest in everything. And you can see the outcome in our numbers. Our arrears numbers are 2.59% sitting against 3.5% for the broader market.

As the market de-risked from that narrative and refocused on company specifics, bonds tightened significantly, delivering spread compression. In an EM portfolio context the bonds acted as a defensive spread stabilizer; in a global investment grade portfolio they also delivered attractive carry income.

So what happened back in 2022? It was a solid company, but the China risk premium got too large. So basically, there were concerns over the China regulations on the internet. So that caused the bonds to be very wide. So as the market derisked from that to focus on the company specifics, the bonds tightened significantly. And that was very good for us as bond holders.

Legal recognition, settlement finality, AML and KYC frameworks must accompany the technology for the system to scale safely.

But actually, the fund itself cannot access underlying basic investment instruments on the blockchain and to invest them until the standard normal operating hours. And that actually impacts the ability for that fund to generate yield for the user.

Without these trust-layer safeguards, participants cannot have the confidence required to move real money at scale. She also argues that AI combined with programmability can shift treasury from reactive to proactive, enabling automated FX and interest rate risk management based on real-time data. quote: We also need to solve for things like regulatory and legal consistency, that's applied as the rails come together and become interoperable. So I'm talking about things like the legal recognition, when we're moving tokenized money and assets on the blockchain, talk about things like settlement finality, and things like any money, anti money laundering and KYC. headline: BOJ hikes inflict greater economic pain than Fed hikes as long-end Japanese borrowing costs surge; yen may continue to weaken despite rate rises, with the BOJ's best relief coming from Fed cuts

So the yen doesn't always get to benefit from the BOJ hikes in the sense that there's economic pain associated with those hikes even though it comes with inflation being tackled. And whilst the fiscal outlook is still unclear and there are risks to it, then the yen could continue to weaken despite and into higher rates. quote: That segment of the market is an incredible attachment point. It allows us to really curate exposure to what I like to call the Goldilocks zone of value creation. By investing in this Goldilocks zone, we avoid much of the cost and risk and duration associated with early stage venture investing while also avoiding much of the valuation and exit environment risk that comes with very late stage investing.

headline: Bearish iron ore call in 2011: aggregate supply growth across BHP and FMG implied two entire Pilbara regions of new supply by 2015, far exceeding realistic Chinese absorption capacity and presaging a price collapse
reasoning: In 2011, bottom-up analysts for BHP and FMG each modelled strong individual production growth — BHP up 20%, FMG up 25% — at a time when world iron ore production had already grown 8.1% or 227mt to 2.8bt. Aggregated, these forecasts implied global iron ore production would reach 3,037bt, an increase of 237mt. The firm estimated that by 2015 the equivalent of two entire Pilbara regions (700mt) of new supply would come to market, with only 420mt (60%) of that realistically absorbable by China. The resulting supply glut was expected to pressure iron ore prices significantly, which is precisely what occurred. This is presented as a historical case study of the Fallacy of Composition — where individually plausible company-level forecasts aggregated to an economically impossible industry outcome.
quote: The reason for our bearish view was that in 2010-11, world iron ore production grew 8.1 per cent or 227mt to 2.8bt. Analysts for BHP and FMG began assuming similar growth levels for 2011-12 – in a classic supply response to the record iron ore prices. BHP production was forecast to grow by 20 per cent, Return On Investment (ROI) by 30 per cent, FMG – 25 per cent. Iron ore production was expected to grow to 3,037bt, an increase of 237mt. Individually each company's future looked bright. But collectively, we estimated that by 2015 'two entire Pilbara regions (700mt) in supply terms will come onto the market. It's a far stretch to expect China to absorb 420mt (60 per cent) of that. The impact we expect is pressure on iron ore prices.' And that's what happened.
episode_title: The Fallacy of Composition

headline: Tech sector operating cash flow forecasts imply an economic impossibility — the Fallacy of Composition — as downstream S&P 500 customer sectors show far lower projected cash flow growth

However, for tech companies to generate those cash flows, their downstream customers must be generating sufficient revenue and cash flow to pay them. Analysts covering the non-tech sectors of the S&P 500 — which are the tech sector's customers — forecast far less incremental operating cash flow. This creates a macro-micro aggregation disconnect: the bullish tech forecasts cannot be reconciled with the more modest forecasts for the rest of the economy. At least one of these groups of analysts must be materially wrong.
quote: Take, for example, the technology analysts. By 2028, they expect operating cash flow to more than double to more than US$2.4 trillion. For companies to generate operating cash flows, they need customers to pay them. Those downstream customers must generate enough revenue and cash flow to pay the upstream suppliers. But analysts covering the other sectors in the S&P 500, which are the technology companies' customers, expect those companies to add far less operating cash flow. In other words, we're seeing another example of the Fallacy of Composition problem. One of the sectors analysts are very wrong. The tech analysts are betting on an explosion of demand for artificial intelligence (AI) services, while the analysts covering the tech companies' customers don't. So, to the tech analysts who aren't aware of the Fallacy of Composition, ask yourselves: where is all this cash going to come from?

reasoning: Tangen notes that shareholder rights — including one share one vote, the ability to influence board composition, and the ability to hold boards accountable — have deteriorated significantly, particularly among new IPOs. And so these rights have deteriorated quite sharply in many countries in the world. And it's a combination of many things. One of them is competition between countries to get the listings, between the various stock exchanges. In Europe, for instance, you have many people choosing Amsterdam because supposedly there are a bit fewer rules there and in some of the other instances.
